transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-07
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~43 minutes
Attendees: Alice Newman (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (CTO, Midwest Savings), Linda Park (Head of Security), Jonah Evans (Compliance), Rachel Kim (Platform)

Summary (auto-generated, brief): discovery on data residency, logging and compliance. Customer is a regional bank evaluating Redwood for chat/agent features in customer support and internal knowledge search. Interested in private deployment and strict logging controls for regulated transactions.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Alice): Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate ya making time. Quick intros then we'll jump to your current constraints around data residency and logs.
00:22 Speaker 2 (Mark): Hi all, Mark here, CTO at Midwest Savings, we run most services in AWS us-east-1 and a smaller EU region for certain products. We're evaluating vendors for LLM features but compliance is the blocker.
00:35 Speaker 1 (Alice): Got it, thanks Mark. Samir, do you want to kick off with a quick overview of the deployment options and what controls we typically provide?
00:45 Speaker 3 (Samir): Sure. Redwood provides three modes: Hosted API (our managed endpoints), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools for a customer in our infra), and Private (customer VPC or on-prem with private control plane). Each has different tradeoffs re: latency, cost, and control over logs/keys.
01:05 Speaker 3 (Samir): For compliance, Private gives the most control: customer-managed KMS, no telemetry leaving the VPC unless configured, and full audit log segregation. Dedicated sits in between: isolated capacity but our control plane still handles routing; you can opt to have limited telemetry. Hosted is fastest to ship but has more shared infrastructure and default logging.
01:35 Speaker 2 (Mark): Okay, when you say "limited telemetry" what exactly can be disabled in Dedicated? We can't have full request/response logs of PII in any vendor logs.
01:45 Speaker 3 (Samir): Right. You can disable request/response logging at the route level, enable redaction, or route logs to your own S3 (or we can push to your account). For Dedicated we support a setting to not persist request/response in our control plane logs; only minimal invocation metadata is kept for billing and telemetry by default.
02:05 Speaker 4 (Linda): To be clear, we also have regulators asking for audit trails. We need access to certain telemetry for incidents and for audits but with strict redaction rules and role-based access.
02:18 Speaker 3 (Samir): Understood. We support RBAC in the Console and audit logs for admin actions. For request-level logs, we can either redact PII at ingest, or not record payloads and instead record hashed references and metadata like model, route, latency, token counts.
02:42 Speaker 2 (Mark): On data residency — we need EU customer data to stay in EU. Do you have an EU-only private deployment?
02:52 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes, we operate regions and can do private control plane deployments in EU. For Private you can run the control plane in your VPC in eu-west-1 and keep everything there. For Dedicated we can provision capacity in a specific region but the control plane still might be in our central region unless you pick Private.
03:12 Speaker 4 (Linda): What about encryption keys? We require customer-managed keys for anything that could be considered sensitive.
03:20 Speaker 3 (Samir): We support CMKs (customer-managed keys) via cloud KMS in Private and Dedicated with VPC options; for Hosted we offer bring-your-own-key for certain enterprise tiers and KMS integrations, but tighter restrictions are available in Private.
03:38 Speaker 5 (Jonah): Are there any logs that are non-optional? Regulator will want proof of certain transactions and we may need request traces for 7 years.
03:48 Speaker 3 (Samir): We can retain admin/audit logs for long windows and export them to your archival storage (S3 with lifecycle). For request traces, we can configure export pipelines to your storage, with redaction rules and legal hold tags; retention is then under your control. But note: storing full plaintext request/response will be a higher risk and may require different contractual terms.
04:16 Speaker 1 (Alice): Also want to call out SOC2 and ISO artefacts — we can share those docs. Many banks ask for SOC2+ISO + pen test reports.
04:26 Speaker 4 (Linda): Yes, please send those. Also network diagrams and our security team will want to see ACLs and flow logs.
04:34 Speaker 1 (Alice): We'll include architecture diagrams and the SOC2/ISO summary.
04:40 Speaker 5 (Jonah): HIPAA — not our primary, but some of our partners handle health-adjacent data, so curious if you support HIPAA BAA?
04:50 Speaker 3 (Samir): We have BAA options for Private deployments; hosted BAA is limited to enterprise engagements. We can discuss scope in the next call.
05:03 Speaker 2 (Mark): Cost is obviously a factor. Private looks great for compliance but is it significantly more expensive and does it add latency?
05:15 Speaker 3 (Samir): Private tends to have higher fixed cost due to reserved infra and network egress patterns, but you get predictable throughput and full control. Latency is usually comparable if deployed regionally close to your users; networking hop changes can add a few tens of ms.
05:40 Speaker 2 (Mark): For customer support use case we care about sub-200ms generation at short seq lengths. Is that realistic in Private?
05:50 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes, with the right C2/C4 instance types and batching configs we see consistent sub-200ms for short responses. We'll want to run a bench in your environment to validate.
06:05 Speaker 4 (Linda): About logging restrictions — we have a policy: certain token patterns (account numbers, SSNs) must never be logged in curious systems. Can your pipeline redact those automatically?
06:18 Speaker 3 (Samir): We have configurable redaction rules and allow regex-based redaction at the ingestion endpoint. You can also route all logs through a gateway in your VPC to perform additional redaction before anything leaves your network.
06:35 Speaker 5 (Jonah): And can we switch off telemetry completely for certain routes?
06:40 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes, you can disable request/response persistence per route; we still record basic usage metrics for billing unless you choose to export raw usage for self-billing.
06:54 Speaker 2 (Mark): Do you support legal holds? We may need to snapshot specific logs for e-discovery.
07:02 Speaker 3 (Samir): We support export + tagging so you can apply legal hold policies in your archival storage. We can also provide snapshots on request via a support process.
07:18 Speaker 1 (Alice): Any integrations you need called out? We can push logs to S3, Splunk, Datadog, or to your SIEM via SNS/Kinesis.
07:29 Speaker 4 (Linda): Splunk is our standard for security ops.
07:32 Speaker 3 (Samir): Great — we have Splunk HEC and forwarder integrations.
07:40 Speaker 2 (Mark): Another question: isolated compute vs shared model weights. Is it possible for you to run a model that is entirely dedicated to us? We worry about cross-tenant leakage.
07:52 Speaker 3 (Samir): For Dedicated and Private we provide isolated model instances and runtime isolation; weights may be the same upstream model but runtime isolation prevents cross-tenant cache leakage. For the highest assurance we offer Private on-prem.
08:10 Speaker 5 (Jonah): On the note of PII in embeddings — if we do embeddings for search, can we prevent raw text from being stored in third-party embedding stores?
08:21 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes — you can configure embeddings not to be persisted in our service and instead push vectors into your own vector DB in your VPC.
08:32 Speaker 2 (Mark): Good. What about GDPR data subject requests — ability to delete a user's data from logs?
08:40 Speaker 3 (Samir): In Private/Dedicated where you control storage, you can honor DSARs directly. For Hosted we have processes to assist but deletion scope depends on what backups and exports exist. We can support selective deletion of request/response if they're in our datastore, but for complete guarantees Private is recommended.
09:05 Speaker 4 (Linda): We also need strong IAM integration — SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC.
09:15 Speaker 3 (Samir): We support SAML SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, and role-based policies at the project/route level.
09:25 Speaker 2 (Mark): Ok, here's a tricky one: our legal team will want to ensure logs that contain CHD never leave our controlled accounts. Can Redwood support a flow where logs are written directly into our AWS account and never to Redwood-managed buckets?
09:38 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes — for Dedicated we can set up log export to your AWS account; for Private it's default. That satisfies the 'never leave our account' requirement.
09:50 Speaker 5 (Jonah): For auditing, will you provide signed attestations or timestamped exports? We need chain-of-custody.
09:58 Speaker 3 (Samir): We can provide signed manifests and use KMS-wrapped exports; in Private you can manage keys and signatures yourself.
10:10 Speaker 1 (Alice): Sounds like folks want artifacts: SOC2, ISO, architecture, sample redaction configs, and a POC scope. We'll compile that.
10:20 Speaker 2 (Mark): Timeline: we're hoping to pilot in Q4 and make a decision by end of year.
10:28 Speaker 1 (Alice): That's tight but doable. We'll prioritize the SE deep-dive and a short POC to validate logs and latency.
10:36 Speaker 5 (Jonah): About POC scope — we need a runbook for audit: what logs are produced, where they're stored, redaction proof, and a way to demonstrate retention windows.
10:50 Speaker 3 (Samir): We'll draft a POC plan: test vectors that include PII patterns, routing to your S3, redaction verification, latency/throughput benchmarks.
11:05 Speaker 4 (Linda): One more: data residency for backups and snapshots — are snapshots encrypted and region-locked?
11:14 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes, snapshots are encrypted with KMS in-region; for Private we ensure snapshots remain in customer region and can be stored in your account.
11:28 Speaker 2 (Mark): Ok, thanks. On encryption at rest and in transit — what cipher suites and key rotation policies do you support?
11:38 Speaker 3 (Samir): We use TLS1.2+/TLS1.3 for transit; at rest we use AES-GCM-256 and KMS-backed keys. We support key rotation via KMS and customers can rotate per their policies.
11:55 Speaker 5 (Jonah): Are there any regulatory controls you don't support today that could be blockers?
12:01 Speaker 3 (Samir): Some extremely prescriptive controls — e.g., certain central bank-specific audit formats — may need custom work. We try to capture those during scoping.
12:12 Speaker 2 (Mark): Fine. Could you share any reference customers in financial services?
12:18 Speaker 1 (Alice): Yes we can share a couple of redacted references and case studies after we get NDA in place.
12:28 Speaker 5 (Jonah): NDA will be fine.
12:33 Speaker 1 (Alice): Anything else from the team?
12:36 Speaker 4 (Linda): Just that we'll want a written runbook and a single point of contact for security questions.
12:43 Speaker 1 (Alice): We'll assign Samir as the security SE contact and I'll be the account AE.
12:50 Speaker 2 (Mark): Sounds good.
13:00 Speaker 1 (Alice): Quick recap / next steps before we close?
13:05 Speaker 3 (Samir): I'll draft the technical deep-dive agenda and the POC plan; include specifics on redaction rules and export flows.
13:12 Speaker 1 (Alice): I'll send SOC2/ISO docs, pricing ballpark, and customer reference request.
13:18 Speaker 5 (Jonah): We'll share compliance checklist and retention windows.
13:24 Speaker 1 (Alice): Target dates: docs by 2025-10-09, POC scope and pricing by 2025-10-10, schedule SE deep-dive week of 2025-10-13.
13:36 Speaker 2 (Mark): Perfect. Thanks everyone.
13:40 Speaker 4 (Linda): Thanks.
13:42 Speaker 1 (Alice): Thanks all, we'll follow up via email.
